nameStory: Reeve's Spirea gets its name from John Reeves, a 19th-century English botanist who collected plants in China. The 'spirea' part comes from the Greek word 'speira' meaning wreath, perfectly describing how the cascading white flowers seem to garland the gracefully arching branches. It's also called 'bridalwreath spirea' because those frothy white blooms look just like decorative wedding garlands.
description: Reeve's Spirea is an ornamental shrub that creates a stunning spring display with its arching branches covered in clusters of snow-white flowers. Growing up to about 5 feet tall, this member of the rose family forms a graceful, fountain-like shape that's wider than it is tall. The flowers appear in small, puffy clusters that look almost like tiny white pompoms scattered along the drooping branches. Though originally from Asia, it's planted in New England gardens where it's prized for its elegant form and reliable spring blooms.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small white flowers cluster in tight, round pompom-like groups along the branches, each individual flower having 5 tiny petals that create a frothy, dense appearance when massed together

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Branches arch gracefully downward in a fountain-like pattern, creating a weeping or cascading effect that's wider than the shrub is tall

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, oval leaves with slightly toothed edges that feel smooth to the touch and alternate along the stems rather than growing in pairs

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Young stems are smooth and reddish-brown, becoming more gray-brown with age, with a clean appearance that lacks thorns despite being in the rose family

habitat: In New England, Reeve's Spirea is found almost exclusively in cultivated settings like home gardens, parks, and landscaped areas rather than growing wild. It thrives in well-drained soils and full to partial sun, often planted as an ornamental border shrub or specimen plant. You're most likely to spot it in suburban neighborhoods and botanical gardens where it's valued for its spring flower display.

seasonality.spring: This is showtime for Reeve's Spirea, with masses of white pompom flower clusters covering the arching branches in May, creating a spectacular bridal-veil effect that's hard to miss.
seasonality.summer: After flowering, the shrub settles into its green foliage phase with small, toothed leaves clothing the graceful arching branches, maintaining its fountain-like shape.
seasonality.fall: Leaves may turn yellowish before dropping, and you might notice small dry seed capsules where the flowers once were, though fall color isn't particularly showy.
seasonality.winter: The bare, arching branch structure creates an elegant sculptural form, with smooth reddish-brown young twigs contrasting against older gray-brown stems.

funFact: Despite being called 'bridalwreath,' Reeve's Spirea flowers have no fragrance at all—unlike many white wedding flowers, these pompom clusters rely purely on their visual drama rather than scent to attract both pollinators and admiring gardeners!
confusionNotes: Reeve's Spirea can be confused with other white-flowered spireas, especially Bridal-wreath Spirea, but Reeve's has distinctly round, pompom-like flower clusters while Bridal-wreath has flatter flower clusters. Remember: 'Reeve's has round puffs' for the pompom effect.
contextualKnowledge: The name 'bridalwreath spirea' is actually shared by several different spirea species, which can be confusing for gardeners and plant enthusiasts. True Bridal-wreath (Spiraea prunifolia) is a different species entirely, though both are commonly planted and both create that cascading white-flowered effect that makes them popular wedding and garden plants.
compareHints: Among the spireas, Reeve's stands out for its distinctly pompom-shaped flower clusters and strongly arching growth habit. While Northern Meadowsweet and White Meadowsweet have upright growth with cone-shaped flower clusters, and Steeplebush has fuzzy pink flowers, Reeve's creates that signature fountain effect with tight, round white flower balls. Japanese Spirea tends to be more upright and often has pink flowers rather than the pure white pompoms of Reeve's.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the meadowsweets, white meadowsweet stands out with its pure white flowers and smooth leaf undersides.
Among the Spiraea species in New England, steeplebush is the only one with distinctly pink, steeple-shaped flower clusters and woolly leaf undersides.
Japanese Spirea differs from native New England spireas like Steeplebush and White Meadowsweet by its compact, mounded garden-shrub appearance and pink flat-topped flower clusters.
Unlike the native white meadowsweet and steeplebush which have single flowers in upright cone-shaped clusters, bridal-wreath has double flowers in rounded clusters along arching branches.
Among the spireas, Thunberg's meadowsweet stands out for its very early bloom time and fine, narrow leaves.
Northern meadowsweet is much shorter and more compact than white meadowsweet, with smaller flower clusters and a preference for cooler locations.
Among New England's spireas, Threelobe Spirea is unique for its three-lobed leaves - all other regional spireas have simple, unlobed leaves.
